Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verses 1–3:

It has been said regarding ﴿Ta Ha﴾ that it is one of the names of the Prophet (ﷺ). It has also been said that its meaning is "O man." See the discussion of the disjointed letters (huruf al-hija') at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah.

﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you that you should be distressed﴾. It has been said that the Prophet (ﷺ) stood in prayer until his feet swelled, so the verse was revealed to lighten the burden upon him. On this view, "distress" (al-shaqa') means excessive exertion in worship. It has also been said that it refers to grief over the disbelief of the disbelievers. The wording is general and includes all of this, and the meaning is that He negated from him every kind of distress in this world and the Hereafter, because the Qur'an was sent down to him, and it is the cause of happiness.

﴿But as a reminder﴾: this is in the accusative as an exception of a disconnected kind (istithna' munqati'). Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for the position of ﴿to be distressed﴾, since that is in the position of an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). Al-Zamakhshari rejected this because the two categories differ. It is also valid for it to be in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, whose sense is: "We sent it down as a reminder."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verses 9–10:

﴿And has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ The phrase is an interrogative, but the purpose of it is to draw attention (al-tanbih). ﴿When he saw a fire﴾ The governing element (al-'amil) of "idh" (when) is "hadith" (the story/narrative), because it carries the meaning of a verb. The story of Moses was that he set out with his family from Madyan, heading for Egypt. He travelled by night and needed a fire. He struck his flint (zinad) but it did not spark, so he saw a fire and made for it, and God called out to him and sent him to Pharaoh. ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾ that is, I saw it. ﴿With a brand﴾ (qabas), which is a burning ember from the fire, held at the top of a stick, a reed, or the like. ﴿With a brand, or I may find at the fire guidance﴾ meaning guidance to the road, from a guide or otherwise.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 12:

﴿So take off your two sandals.﴾ It has been said: he was only commanded to remove his sandals because they were made of the skin of a dead donkey, so he was commanded to remove the impurity. Ibn 'Atiyya (Ibn ʿAṭiyya) chose that he was commanded to remove them in order to show courtesy, to honour the blessed place, and to humble himself in the station of intimate conversation with God. This is the better view. ﴿In the sacred valley﴾, that is, the purified one, ﴿Tuwa﴾. Regarding its meaning there are two opinions. The first is that it is the name of the valley, and its i'rab (grammatical analysis) on this view is in apposition (badal). It may also be read with tanwin (nunation), taking it as a place, or left without tanwin (ghayr munsarif), taking it as a specific spot. The second is that its meaning is "twice," so its i'rab on this view is as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: the valley was sanctified once after another, or Musa was called once after another.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 14:

﴿And establish the prayer for My remembrance﴾. It was said: the meaning is "so that you remember Me in it." It was also said: "so that I may remember you by it." Thus the verbal noun (masdar) is an idafa to the object (mudaf li-l-maf'ul) on the first view, and an idafa to the subject (mudaf li-l-fa'il) on the second. It was also said: the meaning of "for My remembrance" is "at the time of My remembrance," like His saying: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra: 78], i.e., at the decline of the sun. This last view is the most preferred (arjah), because the Prophet ﷺ used this verse as evidence for the obligation of prayer upon one who forgot it when he remembers it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 15:

﴿I am almost going to conceal it﴾. People have disagreed about its meaning. It has been said: "akhfīhā" means "uzhhiruhā" (I make it manifest), and that "akhfā" is among the words with two opposite meanings (al-adrād).

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This view is flawed. The known usage in the language is that one says akhfā, with an alif, from al-ikhfāʾ (concealing), and khafiya, without an alif, meaning "appeared." If it meant manifestation, it would be said as akhfīhā with the hamza of the present tense opened (i.e., ukhfīhā would not apply, rather "ukhfīhā" with fatḥa on the hamza). This is read that way in the irregular (shādhdh) readings." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It has come in some dialects that akhfā means khafiya, i.e., appeared. So this view is not flawed on that dialect."

It has also been said: "akādu" means "uridu" (I intend), so the meaning is "I intend to conceal it." It has also been said: the meaning is "inna al-sāʿata ātiyatun" (the Hour is coming), and the sentence is complete at "akād," meaning "I almost bring it about, because of its nearness"; then He resumed the information and said "akhfīhā." It has also been said: the meaning is "I almost conceal it from myself, so how could I conceal it from you?"

These views are weak. The correct view is that God kept the time of the Hour unspecified, so He did not let anyone know it. He nearly concealed its occurrence because its time was hidden, but He did not conceal it once He informed of its occurrence. So "akhfā" has its known linguistic meaning, and "kāda" has its meaning of approaching something without its actually happening. This meaning is the choice of the verifying scholars (al-muḥaqqiqūn).

﴿That it may be recompensed﴾ is connected to "ātiyatun" (coming). ﴿According to what it strives﴾, i.e., according to what it does.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 39:

﴿Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the river (al-yamm)﴾. The first pronoun refers to Musa, and the second refers to the chest, or to Musa. Al-yamm means the sea, but what is meant here is the Nile. Pharaoh had been told that his destruction and the ruin of his kingdom would come at the hands of a boy from the Children of Israel, so he ordered that every male child born to them be slaughtered. Allah inspired the mother of Musa to place him in the chest and to cast the chest into the river, and she did so. Pharaoh was in a place overlooking the Nile, and he saw the chest, so he ordered it brought to him. It was brought to him, and his wife was with him. He opened it, and his wife felt compassion for him and asked to take him as a son, and he permitted her to do so. ﴿An enemy to Me and an enemy to him will take him﴾: this is Pharaoh. ﴿Love from Me﴾: meaning, I made you beloved. It was also said that it means the love of people for him, since no one would see him without loving him. It was also said that it means the love and mercy of Pharaoh's wife toward him. As for His words ﴿from Me﴾: it may be connected to His words ﴿And I cast upon you﴾, or it may be an attribute of "love," in which case it is connected to a omitted element. ﴿And that you might be raised under My eye﴾: meaning, that you be nurtured and treated well in My sight and under My protection. The governing element for ﴿wa-li-tuṣna'a﴾ (and that you might be raised) is omitted.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verses 58–59:

﴿So set for us a appointment, (a meeting) between us and you﴾ (fa-ij'al bayna-na wa-bayna-ka mawʿidan). The word mawʿid may be an ism al-maṣdar (a verbal noun used as a noun), or an ism al-zaman (a noun of time), or an ism al-makan (a noun of place). That it is a noun of place is indicated by His words ﴿a place, level (and equal)﴾ (makānan suwan), but this is weakened by His words ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾ (mawʿidukum yawmu al-zīna), since He answered with an adverb of time. That it is a noun of time is indicated by His words ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾ (yawmu al-zīna), but this is weakened by His words ﴿a place (makānan) level (suwan)﴾. That it is a verbal noun meaning "promise" is indicated by His words ﴿we will not fail it﴾ (lā nukhlifuhu), because failing (ikhlāf) is attributed only to a promise, not to a time or a place. But this too is weakened by His words ﴿a place﴾ (makānan) and ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾ (yawmu al-zīna). So on every reading there must be either an interpretation (taʾwīl) or an implied element (iḍmār), and the grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) of the word makānan differs according to these readings.

As for when mawʿid is a noun of place, then mawʿidan and makānan are two objects (mafʿūlān) of His words "so set" (fa-ij'al). The words "the Day of Adornment" correspond to this in meaning, not in wording, because gathering at a place necessarily entails a time. If mawʿid is a noun of time, then makānan is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf zaman), and the sense is: an appointment occurring in a place. If mawʿid is a verbal noun, then makānan is in the accusative as an object of the verbal noun mawʿid itself, or of a verb of similar meaning. The words "the Day of Adornment" correspond to this with an omitted genitive construction, its sense being: your appointment is the promise of the Day of Adornment. Al-Ḥasan read "the Day of Adornment" in the accusative, and this corresponds to mawʿid being a verbal noun without any omitted element.

"A place level (suwan)" means: even in distance between us and you. It is said its meaning is: level ground, having neither depression nor elevation. It is recited with the sīn vowelled with kasra and with ḍamma, and the meaning is the same.

"The Day of Adornment" (yawmu al-zīna) is a feast day for them. It is said it was the Day of ʿAshūrāʾ.

"And that the people be gathered" (wa-an yuḥsha) is conjoined to "the adornment" (al-zīna), so it is in the genitive position, or conjoined to "the day" (al-yawm), so it is in the nominative position. Mūsā intended that your appointment be at the gathering of the people in full view, so that his miracle would become manifest and the truth would be made clear to the people.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 20, verses 63–64:**

﴿They said: Indeed these two are certainly magicians.﴾ He recited "inna hadhayn" (إن هذين) with the ya' (ياء), and there is no difficulty in that. He also recited with the lightened inna (إنْ, takhfif), which is the lightened form of the heavy inna (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah, the lightened form of the emphatic particle), and after it hadhani (هذان) is raised as the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence). As for the reading of Nafi' and others, with the heavy inna (إنّ) and hadhani raised, it is said that inna (إنْ) here means "na'am" (نعم, "yes"), so it does not govern the accusative. From this is what is narrated in the hadith that "al-hamd" (الحمد) is in the nominative. It is also said that the subject of inna is the pronoun of the matter and affair, its estimate being "inna al-amr" (إن الأمر, "indeed the matter is"), and "hadhani lasahiranı" (هذان لساحران) is a subject and predicate in the position of the predicate of inna.

It is said that the Qur'an in this verse follows the dialect of Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b (بنو الحارث بن كعب), which is to keep the dual with the alif (ألف) in the accusative and genitive cases. Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "This is among the things in which the scribes of the Mushaf made errors."

﴿And they would take away your ideal way of life.﴾ That is, they would take away your good conduct.

﴿So resolve upon your plot.﴾ That is, determine it and carry it out.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 66:

﴿It is imagined to him, by their magic, that their ropes and staffs are moving.﴾ Some scholars cited this verse as evidence that magic is mere imagination (takhyil) and not reality. Others said: the trick of the magicians in making the ropes and staffs appear to move was that they filled them with mercury (zi'baq), then lit a fire beneath them and covered the fire so that people would not see it. When the mercury felt the heat of the fire or the sun, it flowed, while it was inside the hollow of the ropes and staffs, and so it moved them. Thus it appeared to the people that they were walking. Then Musa threw his staff, and it became a serpent, and it swallowed them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verses 77–79:

﴿That you travel by night with My servants﴾, meaning the Children of Israel, and He attributed them to Himself as an honour to them. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 83:

﴿And what has hastened you from your people, O Moses?﴾ The story behind this verse is that Moses, peace be upon him, when Allah commanded him to set out with the Children of Israel toward Mount Sinai (al-Tur), went ahead of them alone, hastening to obey Allah's command and seeking His pleasure, and he told the Children of Israel to follow after him. He appointed his brother Harun (Aaron) as their deputy. At that time, the Samiri (al-Samiri) commanded them to worship the calf. When Moses arrived at al-Tur ahead of his people, Allah the Exalted said: "What has hastened you from your people?" Allah asked Moses about the reason for his haste ahead of his people only so that Moses would inform Him that they were coming behind him, and then Allah would tell him what they had done after him, namely worshipping the calf. It was also said: He asked him in the manner of censure for his going ahead alone, without his people, so Moses offered two excuses. The first: that his people were "on his track," meaning close behind him, so he had not gone far ahead of them, which would have warranted reproach. The second: that he had only gone ahead seeking the pleasure of Allah.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 20, verses 85–88:

﴿And the Samiri led them astray.﴾ The Samiri (al-Samiri) was a man from the Children of Israel. It is said that he was the son of Musa's maternal uncle. It is also said that he was not of them, but was ascribed to a village in Egypt called Samirah. He was a sorcerer and a hypocrite. ﴿So Musa returned to his people﴾ meaning he returned from Mount Tur after completing the forty days in which Allah spoke with him. ﴿Angry and grieved.﴾ This is mentioned in al-A'raf [7:149].

﴿Did your Lord not promise you a good promise?﴾ meaning what He had promised them of reaching Mount Tur. ﴿Did the time seem long to you?﴾ meaning the duration. This statement is a rebuke to them. ﴿Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord would descend upon you?﴾ [Musa's words are being reported here as well.] ﴿By our having broken our appointment with you﴾ (bi-mulkina) is read with fatha, damma and kasra. Its meaning is: we did not break your appointment by having power over our affair, but we were overcome by the plot of the Samiri. So it may be that they gave as an excuse their lack of power and capacity, and the reading with damma on the mim (mulkina) fits this meaning. They also gave as an excuse their lack of control over themselves in judgment and their failure to be granted sound opinion, and the readings with fatha and kasra (mulkina / milkina) fit this meaning. ﴿We were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people﴾ The "awzar" (burdens) here means loads; they were called awzar because of their weight, or because they gained sins (awzar, i.e. wrongs) through them. The "ornaments of the people" are the jewelry of the Copts, the people of Pharaoh. The Children of Israel had borrowed it from them before their destruction. This is on the basis that the meaning of his words ﴿"follow me"﴾ concerns rebuking and fighting. But had I followed you in walking to the Mount (al-Tur), some of them would have followed me and not others, and their community would have been divided. This is on the basis that the meaning of ﴿"follow me"﴾ concerns walking to the Mount. ﴿"And you did not observe my word."﴾ That is, his words to him: "Take my place among my people and set things right."

﴿He said, "What is your affair, O Samiri?"﴾ That is, Musa said, "What is your matter?" The word *khatb* (affair, matter) implies reproach, because it is used for disagreeable matters. ﴿He said, "I perceived what they did not perceive. So I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger"﴾ That is, I saw what they did not see, namely Jibril (peace be upon him) and his horse. ﴿So I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger﴾ That is, I took a handful of dust from the footprint of the Messenger's horse, and the Messenger is Jibril. Ibn Mas'ud recited "from the footprint of the horse of the Messenger." Jibril was called the Messenger because Allah sent him to Musa. The word *qabdah* (handful) is a verbal noun of *qabada*, and using it to mean the object taken is a case of naming the object by its verbal noun, as in *darb al-amir* (the ruler's striking). It is said *qabada* with the *dad* (ض) when one takes something with the fingers and palm, and with the *sad* (ص) when one takes with the tips of the fingers; the latter has also been recited that way in an irregular recitation (*shadhdh*, a reading not reported with the full chain of transmission). ﴿Then I threw it﴾ That is, I cast it upon the ornaments, so it became a calf, or upon the calf, so it had a lowing sound. ﴿He said, "Go, for you have in this life [the saying], 'No touching.'"﴾ Musa (peace be upon him) punished the Samiri by forbidding people from mixing with him, sitting with him, eating with him, and speaking with him. Along with that, it was made his lot for the rest of his life to say: "No touching," meaning no contact and no harming. It is narrated that if anyone touched him, fever would afflict both him and the one who touched him. So he kept away from the people, and the people kept away from him. ﴿And indeed you have an appointment﴾ meaning the punishment in the Hereafter, and this is a threat and a warning. ﴿Look at your god, to which you remained devoted﴾ The original form of *ẓalta* is *ḍalilta*, with one of the two *lam*s dropped. The original meaning of *ẓalla* is to remain during the day; then it was used for persisting at something by night and by day. ﴿We will surely burn it﴾ from burning with fire. It is also recited with a *fatḥah* on the *nun* and a *ḍammah* on the *ra'*, meaning "we will file it down with a file." Some scholars interpreted the common recitation (*qira'at al-jama'ah*) as having this meaning as well, because gold is not destroyed by burning with fire. The correct view is that the intended meaning of burning it with fire is melting it and destroying its form, so the common recitation can be understood in that sense. ﴿Then we will surely scatter it into the sea, scattering﴾ That is, we will cast it into the sea, and *nasf* is scattering dust and the like. ﴿Your god is only Allah﴾ and the rest of the verse: this is part of Musa's speech to the Children of Israel.

﴿Thus do We relate to you﴾: an address from God Most High to our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and "the news of what has preceded": the accounts of earlier peoples. ﴿A reminder﴾: meaning the Qur'an. ﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾: meaning turning away in denial of it. ﴿A burden﴾: "wizr" (burden) in the language means weight, and here it means punishment, as in His saying ﴿abiding therein﴾; or it means sins, because they are the cause of punishment. ﴿And evil will it be for them on the Day of Resurrection, a load﴾: the burden is likened to a load because of its heaviness. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿evil will it be﴾ runs in the manner of "bi'sa" (how evil), so its subject is a hidden pronoun explained by ﴿a load﴾. And one reading has "nunfikh" (We blow) with the nun, meaning by Our command. ﴿Blue-eyed﴾: that is, of blue colour like blackness; and it was said: blue eyes from blindness.

Surah 20 (Ta-Ha), verse 107:

﴿Thou wilt not see therein any crookedness﴾ (ʿiwaj). It is well known in the language that ʿiwaj, with a kasra on the ʿayn, is used for abstract meanings, while ʿawaj, with a fatha on the ʿayn, is used for concrete things and for the earth itself being uneven. So the original form would have been to say it with a fatha, but He said it with a kasra for emphasis in negating it, since what is abstract is finer than what is concrete. Thus He negated it to make it the utmost in negating crookedness in every respect. ﴿Nor any elevation﴾ (amt). Al-amt is a slight rise.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 108:

﴿They will follow the summoner﴾, meaning the one who calls the creatures to the gathering (al-hashr), ﴿with no deviation (ʿiwaj) for him﴾, i.e., no one will deviate from following him and walking toward his voice; or, there is no crookedness in his call, because it is the truth. ﴿Whispering (hamsan)﴾ is the faint, low sound.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 109:

﴿No intercession will benefit except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and whose word He approves.﴾

It is possible that the exception (istithna') is connected (muttasil), with "man" (من) in the accusative position as the object of "tanfa'" (benefit), and the object is the one for whom intercession is made (al-mashfu' lah). The meaning then is: intercession benefits no one except the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted that intercession be made. It is also possible that the exception is disconnected (munqati'), with "man" referring to the intercessor (al-shafi'), and the meaning is: "But whoever the Most Merciful has permitted, [he] will intercede." ﴿And He approves his word.﴾ If by "the one whom the Most Merciful has permitted" is meant the one for whom intercession is made (al-mashfu' fihi), then the "lam" in "lahu" means "for his sake," i.e., He approves the intercessor's word for the sake of the one for whom intercession is made. If by it is meant the intercessor, then the meaning is that He approves his word in intercession.

The pronouns refer to all of creation. The meaning is as mentioned in the Verse of the Throne: ﴿and they do not encompass Him in knowledge﴾. It has been said that the meaning is: they do not encompass His known things, like His saying: ﴿and they do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. But the correct view in my opinion is that the meaning is: they do not encompass knowledge of His essence, since none knows God in reality except God. Had He intended the first meaning, He would have said "and they do not encompass His action (ʿamal)." That is why He made the exception "except what He wills" there, and did not make an exception here.

﴿And faces will be humbled﴾, meaning they will be humiliated on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Nor fear any injustice or diminishment﴾, meaning any reduction or loss of their good deeds. ﴿Or it will bring them a reminder﴾, meaning a remembrance. "We had already made a covenant with Adam" (ʿahidnā ilā Ādam): that is, We enjoined him that he should not eat from the tree. "But he forgot" (fa-nasiya): this may be forgetfulness, the opposite of remembering, in which case it is an excuse for Adam; or it may mean abandonment (al-tark). Qur'an 20:117: "So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, for then you would be wretched."

That is, do not obey him, lest he drive you both out of the Garden. Here the effect (the cause of expulsion) is put in place of the cause (obedience to Satan). He singled out Adam with the words "then you would be wretched" because he was the one first addressed and the intended subject of the speech. It was also said: the wretchedness of earthly livelihood (ma'ishah) is specific to men.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verses 123–124:

﴿ٱهْبِطَا﴾ ("Go down"): an address to Adam and Eve.

﴿فَإِمَّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُم﴾ ("Then if there comes to you"): here "in" (إن) is the conditional particle, to which the superfluous "ma" (ما) has been attached. Its answer is ﴿فَمَنِ ٱتَّبَعَ﴾ ("whoever follows") ﴿فَلاَ يَضِلُّ وَلاَ يَشْقَىٰ﴾ ("then he will not go astray, nor will he be distressed"), meaning he will not go astray in this world and will not be wretched in the Hereafter.

﴿مَعِيشَةً ضَنكاً﴾ ("a life of hardship"): that is, constricted. It has been said that this refers to the present world, since the disbeliever's livelihood is constricted by his intense greed, even if his material circumstances are comfortable. One of the Sufis said: "No one turns away from the remembrance of Allah except that his time becomes dark for him and his life becomes troubled." It has also been said that this refers to the barzakh (the intermediate state between death and resurrection), and that it refers to Hell, through eating from the zaqqum tree. But this is weak, because after this, the Day of Resurrection and the punishment of the Hereafter are mentioned.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 128:

﴿Afa-lam yahdi lahum﴾ means: "Did it not become clear to them?" The pronoun refers to the Quraysh, and the subject of yahdi (يهد) is implied, its meaning being: "Or did guidance, or the matter, not become clear to them?" Al-Zamakhshari said: the subject is the clause that follows it. It was also said: the subject is the pronoun of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and what supports this is the reading ﴿Afa-lam nahdi﴾ with the nun (نهد). The Kufans said: the subject is kam (كم), ﴿how many﴾ [of the generations destroyed before them]. ﴿Yamshuna fi masakinihim﴾ means: the Quraysh walk through the dwelling places of 'Ad and Thamud, witnessing the traces of their destruction. ﴿Li-uli al-nuha﴾ means: for those possessing intellects (ʿuqul).

**Translation:**

﴿Had it not been for a word that had preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable﴾. The "word" here is the prior decree. The meaning is: had it not been for God's decree to delay the punishment from them, the punishment would have been ﴿inevitable﴾, meaning that it would have befallen them. ﴿And a specified term﴾ is coordinated with ﴿a word﴾: that is, had it not been for the word and the specified term, the punishment would have been inevitable. He delayed it only so that the endings of the verses (ra'us al-ayat, the rhymed verse-endings, known as fawasil) would be balanced. The "specified term" is the Day of Badr, and this interpretation is transmitted in al-Bukhari (al-Bukhari, the hadith compiler). It has also been said that it refers to the term of death, and it has been said that it refers to the Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 130:

﴿And glorify (sabbih) with the praise of your Lord⦆ It is possible that by tasbih (glorification) he means the prayer, or the saying "Subhan Allah," which is the apparent sense of the wording. ﴿With the praise of your Lord﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while you are praising your Lord for having enabled you to glorify Him. It is also possible that the meaning is: glorify Him with a glorification joined with the praise of your Lord, so that it is a command to combine his saying "Subhan Allah" with his saying "al-hamdu lillah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Subhan Allah and al-hamdu lillah fill what is between the heavens and the earth."

﴿Before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾ is a reference to the five obligatory prayers according to those who say that the meaning of ﴿fa-sabbih﴾ is the prayer. So the one before the rising of the sun is the Dawn (Subh) prayer, and the one before its setting is the Noon (Zuhr) and Afternoon ('Asr) prayers. And ﴿from the hours of the night﴾ refers to the Sunset (Maghrib) and Night ('Isha') prayers, and ﴿the ends of the day﴾ refers to the Maghrib and Dawn prayers. He repeated the Dawn prayer in this to emphasize the command to perform it. He called the two extremes "ends" (atraf) for one of two reasons: either as in the expression "fa-qad sagha qulubukuma" (your hearts have inclined), or because the word "day" (nahar) is taken as a generic noun, so that each day has an end, and the "hours of the night" (ana' al-layl) are its periods, the singular of which is ini (إني).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verse 131:

﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ This was mentioned in al-Hijr [88]. Extending the eyes means prolonging the gaze, and this indicates that a gaze that is not prolonged is pardoned. ﴿The splendour of the worldly life﴾ He likened the blessings of this world to blossom (zahr), which is the flower, because blossom has an attractive appearance, then it wilts and perishes. Regarding the accusative case of zahrah there are five possibilities: that it is governed by a concealed verb on the basis of dispraise (dhamm); or that ﴿We bestowed﴾ (matta'na) is taken to include the meaning of "We gave" (a'taynā), so that zahrah is its second object; or that it is a substitute (badal) for the place of the prepositional phrase; or that it is a substitute for azwājan, on the assumption of "those possessing a splendour"; or that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl).

﴿So that We may test them therein﴾ That is, so that We may try them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 20, verses 132–133:

﴿We do not ask you for provision﴾ meaning: We do not ask you to provide for yourself or for your family, so that you and your family may be free for prayer; it is We who provide for you. Some of the salaf, when their household was in want, would say: "Get up and pray, for Allah has commanded you with this," and he would recite this verse: ﴿And has there not come to them clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ Here "clear evidence" (al-bayyina) means proof, and "the former scriptures" (al-suhuf al-ula) are the Torah, the Gospel and other books of Allah. The meaning of this answer is: There has come to you proof of what is in the Torah and the Gospel concerning the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ), so why do you seek another sign?

It is also possible that the meaning is: The Qur'an has come to you, and in it are the sciences and stories that are in the former scriptures, and that is a clear evidence and proof that it is from Allah.
